meta.title: Lawn Mowing Experiment
meta.description: This is a story about how our minds work.
meta.byline: By Russell Samora, Arjun Kakkar, Florina Sutanto, and Sushant Karki

value.prompt: Let’s start with a game: how efficiently can you mow this lawn?
value.played: A little while ago, you mowed this lawn. Here’s a replay.

value.b2: The most efficient path is just
value.skip: You skipped the game, so here is just the optimal path. Is this what you would’ve done?
value.strip: If we strip away the grass, mowing is really just a path of connected squares.

content.value: A few weeks ago, 20,305 people mowed the same lawn. Here is every path they took.
<mark>visual of all paths</mark>
Many came close to the optimal path. 55% of people came within five moves of the best possible path, and 18% did it perfectly.
<mark>histogram of moves</mark>

Many different approaches, yet similar, pretty good outcomes. Only 49 squares needed to be covered, but people found 9,640 different ways to do it. Despite all that variety, the median person still hit 91% efficiency (within 5 moves).
For this small lawn, there were 12 different perfect solutions and people found them all.
<mark>visual all 12</mark>
But what were you actually solving?
Finding the best path through the squares is a classic computer science problem. No, don’t leave! We promise this won’t get too wonky.
Path planning problems
Solving the lawn mowing problem is formally called Coverage Path Planning, and is related to one of the most famous path planning problems in computer science: The Traveling Salesman Problem.

value.figcaption: From The Coding Train with Daniel Shiffman

content.value: The premise is simple: a salesman must visit a set of cities exactly once and return to their starting point, all while taking the shortest possible route. We see this all the time in the real world. A pizza delivery driver planning their stops or a trick-or-treater maximizing their candy haul is solving a version of this problem.

We wanted to create this mowing experiment after we read a study that found humans come impressively close to computer-calculated optimal solutions to this problem with fewer stops, and even do pretty good — just 11% less efficient than optimal — for 70+ stops. But as the stops increase, humans’ ability decreases. Would results be similar for mowing a lawn?

value.alt: A chart depicting how people perform on the Traveling Salesman Problem compared to the optimal path, which shows that people perform near-ideal at fewer nodes, with a slow increasing deviation as more nodes are added
value.figcaption: Chart of findings from this study

content.value: A slight detour, if we may. It is worth noting that there are two main ways to tackle a problem like this:

li: algorithms which calculate the optimal path and
heuristics which are simple strategies to complete the path

content.value: Why do we need heuristics? If we look at the brute force calculations for a salesperson visiting just 10 cities, we’d surprisingly need to test 3.6 million possible routes. That number explodes exponentially as more cities are added.
15 cities and we’re at 1.3 trillion possible routes. 😱
20 cities balloons to 2.4 quintillion possible routes. 🤯

When problems are small, the approach doesn’t matter much, almost everything works. But as complexity grows, optimal becomes impossible and heuristics become necessary. This is true for both humans and computers. We both fall back on good-enough strategies when perfect is impractical.
With the maths out of the way we can get back to the good stuff.
The results
Let’s answer the initial driving question: did efficiency decrease as the problem size increased? No!
6,589 people completed all five increasingly-sized lawns in our experiment. Here is a chart of their efficiency across each.
<mark>visual</mark>
On a small lawn, most people found a good solution fast, without much effort. That’s because the challenge was simple enough that the working memory could keep the entire problem in view at once.
<mark>example/visual proof?</mark>

Increase the lawn size and the choices build up quicker than working memory can hold. Should you go down? Where does that leave you 20 moves from now? Would left have been better? Since you can’t see it all at once anymore, your brain does two things:

li: Decomposition: it breaks the problem down into smaller, more manageable chunks. It solves the first one, then moves on to the next.
Compression: it reuses what worked. Patterns and strategies carried over from smaller to larger lawns, which is why people stayed about as efficient even when the lawn got harder.

content.value: An algorithm isn’t bound by a working memory limit. It can follow every possible move to the end and throw out the dead ends. But all this exhaustive work comes at a computational cost.
Seeing people think
We recorded the timestamps of every move, so every time a person hesitated, changed direction, or doubled back, they left a trace.

Let’s walk through level X to see these decisions in action. Everyone mows the easy stretch the same way because there is nothing to decide. At the corner, you can see a fork where people make the first major decision; down or left?
<mark>visual branching diagram</mark>
Expanded to the rest of the lawn, you can see hotspots around the hard parts, and little variation in the open areas.
Thinking barely pays off
We expected people who paused the longest to end up with the best paths, but that’s not what happened.
If we plot pause time vs. efficiency, you can see that pausing doesn’t improve things. Staring longer at the lawn did not make people meaningfully better at mowing it.
<mark>visual scatter, total pause time vs efficiency</mark>

But the pauses were not random. When we map where people stopped, the hesitation piles up in the same spots: next to obstacles, at corners, along edges, and at those moments when you realize you have painted yourself toward a dead end. Pauses are a map of difficulty that mark the forks from the last section, the places where paths diverged.
<mark>visual pause heatmap over the grid</mark>
So thinking did not improve people’s score much, but it did happen exactly where the problem got hard. This raised the question: if pausing does not help, why does anyone win?
Cream of the crop

The best solvers were not the fastest, and they were not the longest thinkers. Speed alone did not predict a good path. Total thinking time did not either. What separated the top solvers was where they spent their attention.

The best mowers moved at about the same pace as everyone else, sometimes slower, but they revisited far fewer cells. They were not burning time everywhere. They were spending it at the forks and cruising through the rest.
<mark>visual  two ghost mowers side by side, top solver vs average, same clock</mark>

So it mattered more when you think, not thinking more or thinking faster. This is exactly what a good heuristic does. It saves your effort for the decisions that matter and spends nothing on the ones that do not.
